stem: If \(a, b, c\) are sides of a triangle and \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\), name the type of triangle:
solution: By the converse of Pythagoras' theorem, if the square of the longest side equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides, i.e. \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\), then the triangle is right angled (with the right angle opposite side \(c\)). Hence the answer is (C) Right angled triangle.

stem: Chords AB and CD of a circle intersect inside the circle at point E. If \(AE = 4\), \(EB = 10\), \(CE = 8\), then find ED:
solution: By the theorem of internal division of two chords, \(AE \times EB = CE \times ED\). So \(4 \times 10 = 8 \times ED\), giving \(ED = \dfrac{40}{8} = 5\). Hence the answer is (B) 5.

stem: Co-ordinates of the origin are ________.
solution: The origin is the point of intersection of the X-axis and the Y-axis; both of its co-ordinates are zero. Hence the co-ordinates of the origin are \((0, 0)\), option (A).

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: If the radius of the base of a cone is 7 cm and its height is 24 cm, then find its slant height:
solution: Slant height \(l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{7^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{49 + 576} = \sqrt{625} = 25\) cm. Hence the answer is (D) 25 cm.

subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: If \(\triangle ABC \sim \triangle PQR\) and \(\dfrac{A(\triangle ABC)}{A(\triangle PQR)} = \dfrac{16}{25}\), then find \(AB : PQ\).
solution: For similar triangles, the ratio of areas equals the ratio of the squares of the corresponding sides: \(\dfrac{A(\triangle ABC)}{A(\triangle PQR)} = \dfrac{AB^2}{PQ^2}\). So \(\dfrac{AB^2}{PQ^2} = \dfrac{16}{25}\), hence \(\dfrac{AB}{PQ} = \sqrt{\dfrac{16}{25}} = \dfrac{4}{5}\). Therefore \(AB : PQ = 4 : 5\).

stem: In \(\triangle RST\), \(\angle S = 90^\circ\), \(\angle T = 30^\circ\), \(RT = 12\) cm, then find RS.
solution: In \(\triangle RST\), \(\angle S = 90^\circ\), so RT is the hypotenuse. Side RS is opposite \(\angle T = 30^\circ\). By the 30\(^\circ\)-60\(^\circ\)-90\(^\circ\) theorem, the side opposite the \(30^\circ\) angle is half the hypotenuse: \(RS = \dfrac{1}{2} \times RT = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 12 = 6\) cm.

stem: If the radius of a circle is 5 cm, then find the length of the longest chord of the circle.
solution: The longest chord of a circle is its diameter. Diameter \(= 2 \times \text{radius} = 2 \times 5 = 10\) cm. So the length of the longest chord is 10 cm.

stem: Find the distance between the points \(O(0, 0)\) and \(P(3, 4)\).
solution: By the distance formula, \(OP = \sqrt{(3 - 0)^2 + (4 - 0)^2} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = \sqrt{25} = 5\) units.

stem: In the given figure, points L, M, N lie on a circle and \(\angle L = 35^\circ\). Complete the activity to find (i) \(m(\text{arc } MN)\) and (ii) \(m(\text{arc } MLN)\).
solution: (i) By the inscribed angle theorem, \(\angle L = \dfrac{1}{2}\, m(\text{arc } MN)\). \(\therefore 35^\circ = \dfrac{1}{2}\, m(\text{arc } MN)\), so \(m(\text{arc } MN) = 2 \times 35^\circ = 70^\circ\). (ii) By the definition of measure of an arc, \(m(\text{arc } MLN) = 360^\circ - m(\text{arc } MN) = 360^\circ - 70^\circ = 290^\circ\).
figureNote: Circle with inscribed triangle LMN; vertex L at the top with the angle 35 degrees marked at L; M at lower-left and N at lower-right on the circle; centre dot shown inside. p-03

stem: Show that \(\cot\theta + \tan\theta = \csc\theta \times \sec\theta\).
solution: L.H.S. \(= \cot\theta + \tan\theta = \dfrac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta} + \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta} = \dfrac{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta \times \cos\theta}\). Since \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\), this \(= \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta \times \cos\theta} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta} \times \dfrac{1}{\cos\theta} = \csc\theta \times \sec\theta = \) R.H.S. \(\therefore \cot\theta + \tan\theta = \csc\theta \times \sec\theta\).

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: Complete the activity to find the surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm. \(\left(\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}\right)\)
solution: Surface area of sphere \(= 4\pi r^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7^2 = 4 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 4 \times 22 \times 7 = 616\) sq.cm.

stem: In trapezium ABCD, side AB \(\parallel\) side PQ \(\parallel\) side DC, with P on side AD and Q on side BC. \(AP = 15\), \(PD = 12\), \(QC = 14\). Find BQ.
solution: Since AB \(\parallel\) PQ \(\parallel\) DC, by the property of three parallel lines and their transversals, \(\dfrac{AP}{PD} = \dfrac{BQ}{QC}\). \(\therefore \dfrac{15}{12} = \dfrac{BQ}{14}\), so \(BQ = \dfrac{15 \times 14}{12} = \dfrac{210}{12} = 17.5\) cm.
figureNote: Trapezium ABCD (A top-left, B top-right, D bottom-left, C bottom-right) with segment PQ drawn parallel to AB and DC; P on side AD, Q on side BC. p-05. NOTE: the value of AP is partly cut at the right page margin; read as 15 (the standard value for this problem) - please verify against the source.

stem: Find the length of the diagonal of a rectangle whose length is 35 cm and breadth is 12 cm.
solution: The diagonal of a rectangle is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the length and the breadth. Diagonal \(= \sqrt{35^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{1225 + 144} = \sqrt{1369} = 37\) cm.

subtopic: Measure of an Arc and Central Angle
stem: In the given figure, points G, D, E, F lie on a circle with centre C. \(\angle ECF = 70^\circ\) and \(m(\text{arc } DGF) = 200^\circ\). Find (i) \(m(\text{arc } DE)\) and (ii) \(m(\text{arc } DEF)\).
solution: The central angle \(\angle ECF = 70^\circ\), so \(m(\text{arc } EF) = 70^\circ\). The whole circle measures \(360^\circ\) and \(m(\text{arc } DGF) = 200^\circ\), so \(m(\text{arc } DEF) = 360^\circ - m(\text{arc } DGF) = 360^\circ - 200^\circ = 160^\circ\). Arc DEF is made up of arc DE and arc EF, so \(m(\text{arc } DE) = m(\text{arc } DEF) - m(\text{arc } EF) = 160^\circ - 70^\circ = 90^\circ\). \(\therefore\) (i) \(m(\text{arc } DE) = 90^\circ\) and (ii) \(m(\text{arc } DEF) = 160^\circ\).
figureNote: Circle with centre C; points G (upper-right), D (upper-left), E (lower-left), F (lower) on the circle; radii CD, CE, CF drawn; angle ECF marked at centre. p-06

stem: Show that the points \(A(-1, -1)\), \(B(0, 1)\), \(C(1, 3)\) are collinear.
solution: By the distance formula: \(AB = \sqrt{(0 - (-1))^2 + (1 - (-1))^2} = \sqrt{1 + 4} = \sqrt{5}\); \(BC = \sqrt{(1 - 0)^2 + (3 - 1)^2} = \sqrt{1 + 4} = \sqrt{5}\); \(AC = \sqrt{(1 - (-1))^2 + (3 - (-1))^2} = \sqrt{4 + 16} = \sqrt{20} = 2\sqrt{5}\). Since \(AB + BC = \sqrt{5} + \sqrt{5} = 2\sqrt{5} = AC\), the points A, B and C are collinear.

stem: A person is standing at a distance of 50 m from a temple looking at its top. The angle of elevation is \(45^\circ\). Find the height of the temple.
solution: Let the height of the temple be \(h\) m. \(\tan 45^\circ = \dfrac{\text{height}}{\text{distance}} = \dfrac{h}{50}\). Since \(\tan 45^\circ = 1\), we get \(1 = \dfrac{h}{50}\), so \(h = 50\) m. The height of the temple is 50 m.

stem: In \(\triangle PQR\), seg PM is a median. The angle bisectors of \(\angle PMQ\) and \(\angle PMR\) intersect side PQ and side PR in points X and Y respectively. Complete the activity to prove that XY \(\parallel\) QR.
solution: In \(\triangle PMQ\), ray MX is the bisector of \(\angle PMQ\). \(\therefore\) by the theorem of angle bisector, \(\dfrac{MP}{MQ} = \dfrac{PX}{XQ}\) ... (I). Similarly, in \(\triangle PMR\), ray MY is the bisector of \(\angle PMR\). \(\therefore \dfrac{MP}{MR} = \dfrac{PY}{YR}\) ... (II). But M is the midpoint of QR, so \(MQ = MR\), giving \(\dfrac{MP}{MQ} = \dfrac{MP}{MR}\) ... (III). From (I), (II) and (III), \(\dfrac{PX}{XQ} = \dfrac{PY}{YR}\). \(\therefore\) by the converse of the basic proportionality theorem, XY \(\parallel\) QR.
figureNote: Triangle PQR with P at the apex, Q at bottom-left, R at bottom-right; M is the midpoint of QR (median PM drawn); a line XY cuts PQ at X and PR at Y and is parallel to QR; dashed segments MX and MY drawn; equal tick marks on QM and MR. p-07

stem: Find the co-ordinates of point P, where P is the midpoint of the line segment AB with \(A(-4, 2)\) and \(B(6, 2)\).
solution: By the midpoint formula, \(P = \left(\dfrac{x_1 + x_2}{2}, \dfrac{y_1 + y_2}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{-4 + 6}{2}, \dfrac{2 + 2}{2}\right) = \left(\dfrac{2}{2}, \dfrac{4}{2}\right) = (1, 2)\). The co-ordinates of the midpoint P are \((1, 2)\).

stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), seg AP is a median. If \(BC = 18\) and \(AB^2 + AC^2 = 260\), find AP.
solution: By Apollonius' theorem, \(AB^2 + AC^2 = 2AP^2 + 2\left(\dfrac{BC}{2}\right)^2\). \(\therefore 260 = 2AP^2 + 2\left(\dfrac{18}{2}\right)^2 = 2AP^2 + 2 \times 81 = 2AP^2 + 162\). So \(2AP^2 = 260 - 162 = 98\), \(AP^2 = 49\), \(AP = 7\) cm.

stem: Prove that, "Angles inscribed in the same arc are congruent."
solution: Let \(\angle PQR\) and \(\angle PSR\) be two angles inscribed in the same arc, both subtending arc PR. By the inscribed angle theorem, an inscribed angle equals half the measure of its intercepted arc. \(\therefore \angle PQR = \dfrac{1}{2}\, m(\text{arc } PR)\) and \(\angle PSR = \dfrac{1}{2}\, m(\text{arc } PR)\). Since both angles equal \(\dfrac{1}{2}\, m(\text{arc } PR)\), we get \(\angle PQR = \angle PSR\). Hence angles inscribed in the same arc are congruent.

subtopic: Construction of a Tangent to a Circle
stem: Draw a circle of radius 3.3 cm. Draw a chord PQ of length 6.6 cm. Draw tangents to the circle at points P and Q.
solution: Steps of construction: (1) Draw a circle with centre O and radius 3.3 cm. (2) Since the required chord \(PQ = 6.6\) cm \(= 2 \times 3.3\) cm, PQ is a diameter; draw a diameter and label its end points P and Q. (3) Draw ray OP and construct a line perpendicular to OP at P — this is the tangent at P. (4) Draw ray OQ and construct a line perpendicular to OQ at Q — this is the tangent at Q. Since PQ is a diameter, OP and OQ are opposite rays, so the tangents at P and Q are parallel to each other.

stem: The radii of the circular ends of a frustum are 14 cm and 6 cm respectively and its height is 6 cm. Find its curved surface area. \((\pi = 3.14)\)
solution: For a frustum, slant height \(l = \sqrt{h^2 + (R - r)^2} = \sqrt{6^2 + (14 - 6)^2} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = \sqrt{100} = 10\) cm. Curved surface area \(= \pi (R + r) l = 3.14 \times (14 + 6) \times 10 = 3.14 \times 20 \times 10 = 628\) sq.cm.

subtopic: Theorem of Areas of Similar Triangles
stem: In \(\triangle ABC\), seg DE \(\parallel\) side BC. If \(2A(\triangle ADE) = A(\square DBCE)\), find \(AB : AD\) and show that \(BC = \sqrt{3}\, DE\).
solution: \(A(\square DBCE) = A(\triangle ABC) - A(\triangle ADE)\). Given \(2A(\triangle ADE) = A(\square DBCE) = A(\triangle ABC) - A(\triangle ADE)\), so \(3A(\triangle ADE) = A(\triangle ABC)\), i.e. \(\dfrac{A(\triangle ADE)}{A(\triangle ABC)} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). Since DE \(\parallel\) BC, \(\triangle ADE \sim \triangle ABC\), and the ratio of areas equals the ratio of squares of corresponding sides: \(\dfrac{AD^2}{AB^2} = \dfrac{DE^2}{BC^2} = \dfrac{1}{3}\). \(\therefore \dfrac{AD}{AB} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), so \(AB : AD = \sqrt{3} : 1\). Also \(\dfrac{DE}{BC} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\), hence \(BC = \sqrt{3}\, DE\).

stem: \(\triangle SHR \sim \triangle SVU\). In \(\triangle SHR\), \(SH = 4.5\) cm, \(HR = 5.2\) cm, \(SR = 5.8\) cm and \(\dfrac{SH}{SV} = \dfrac{3}{5}\). Construct \(\triangle SVU\).
solution: Since \(\dfrac{SH}{SV} = \dfrac{3}{5}\), we have \(\dfrac{SV}{SH} = \dfrac{5}{3}\), so \(\triangle SVU\) is larger than \(\triangle SHR\) with scale factor \(\dfrac{5}{3}\). Steps: (1) Construct \(\triangle SHR\) with \(SH = 4.5\) cm, \(HR = 5.2\) cm, \(SR = 5.8\) cm. (2) Draw ray SB making an acute angle with side SR, on the side opposite to H. (3) Mark 5 equal points \(S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4, S_5\) on ray SB. (4) Join \(S_3 R\). Through \(S_5\) draw a line parallel to \(S_3 R\) meeting ray SR (extended) at U. (5) Through U draw a line parallel to HR meeting ray SH (extended) at V. Then \(\triangle SVU\) is the required triangle similar to \(\triangle SHR\) with \(\dfrac{SV}{SH} = \dfrac{5}{3}\).

subtopic: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
stem: An ice-cream pot has a right circular cylindrical shape. The radius of the base is 12 cm and the height is 7 cm. This pot is completely filled with ice-cream. The entire ice-cream is given to students in the form of right circular ice-cream cones having diameter 4 cm and height 3.5 cm. If each student is given one cone, how many students can be served?
solution: Volume of the cylindrical pot \(= \pi r^2 h = \pi \times 12^2 \times 7 = 1008\pi\) cubic cm. For each cone, radius \(= \dfrac{4}{2} = 2\) cm and height \(= 3.5\) cm, so volume of one cone \(= \dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 2^2 \times 3.5 = \dfrac{14\pi}{3}\) cubic cm. Number of students \(= \dfrac{\text{volume of pot}}{\text{volume of one cone}} = \dfrac{1008\pi}{\frac{14\pi}{3}} = \dfrac{1008 \times 3}{14} = 216\). Hence 216 students can be served.

stem: In the given figure, a circle touches side BC of \(\triangle ABC\) at point P from outside the triangle. Lines AC and AB, when extended, are tangents to the circle at points N and M respectively. Prove that \(AM = \dfrac{1}{2}(\text{Perimeter of } \triangle ABC)\).
solution: By the tangent segment theorem, the two tangent segments drawn to a circle from an external point are equal. From A: \(AM = AN\). From B: \(BM = BP\). From C: \(CN = CP\). Now \(AM + AN = (AB + BM) + (AC + CN) = AB + AC + BM + CN = AB + AC + BP + CP = AB + AC + (BP + PC) = AB + AC + BC = \text{Perimeter of } \triangle ABC\). Since \(AM = AN\), \(2AM = \text{Perimeter of } \triangle ABC\), hence \(AM = \dfrac{1}{2}(\text{Perimeter of } \triangle ABC)\).
figureNote: Triangle ABC with vertex A at the left; a circle lies to the right and touches line BC at point P; side AB extended is tangent to the circle at M (lower point), side AC extended is tangent at N (upper point); centre of the circle marked; B and C are the near vertices with P on segment BC extended region. p-10

stem: Eliminate \(\theta\) if \(x = r\cos\theta\) and \(y = r\sin\theta\).
solution: Squaring and adding: \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\cos^2\theta + r^2\sin^2\theta = r^2(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta) = r^2 \times 1 = r^2\). \(\therefore x^2 + y^2 = r^2\).
